paragraphs.text: For most of human history the sea has been the cheapest road between places, and it has also been the least forgiving. Tens of thousands of merchant ships are thought to have gone down in the Mediterranean alone before the modern era, and the great majority of them carried nothing more remarkable than jars of oil, bundles of cloth and sacks of grain. To an archaeologist, however, such an ordinary cargo is exactly what makes a wreck valuable. A city excavated on land is the record of centuries piled on top of one another, disturbed by every generation that rebuilt it; a ship that sank in an afternoon is a single moment, sealed and left untouched, in which every object was in use on the same day.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The difficulty is that this moment is not preserved evenly. What survives on the seabed depends less on what the ship carried than on where it came to rest. Wood that settles into fine mud, cut off from oxygen, can last for thousands of years, because the organisms that would otherwise consume it cannot live there; the same timber lying on rock in shallow, warm water may disappear within a few decades, eaten by shipworm. Metal corrodes into shapeless lumps, and glass slowly flakes away. Pottery, by contrast, is almost indestructible, and so the typical ancient wreck is found not as a ship but as a mound of broken jars, with the hull, if it survives at all, lying flattened underneath.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Those jars, known as amphorae, are the archaeologist’s most useful witness. Their shapes changed from one region and century to another in ways that are now well catalogued, so that a single handle can often indicate where a vessel was made and roughly when. Many were stamped by the workshop that produced them, and residues trapped in the clay can reveal whether they held wine, fish sauce or olive oil. When hundreds of jars from several different workshops are found together, they allow researchers to reconstruct the route that a ship had taken, since a captain who loaded goods at three harbours left a sample of each in the hold.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, excavating such a site meant divers working in short shifts at depths where the pressure limited them to minutes rather than hours. The work was slow, and positions had to be recorded with tape measures and pencils on plastic boards, which introduced errors that could not later be checked. The last three decades have changed the method almost entirely. Remotely operated vehicles can now work at depths that no diver could reach, and a technique that assembles thousands of overlapping photographs into a three-dimensional model allows an entire site to be measured to within a few millimetres before a single object is lifted. Deep water has also turned out to be kinder to wrecks than shallow water: beyond the reach of anchors, nets and souvenir hunters, some sites have lain almost exactly as they settled.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: What the wrecks have revealed is often at odds with the picture drawn from written sources. Ancient authors wrote mostly about the grain fleets that supplied great cities and about luxury goods, because these interested the governments and wealthy readers for whom they wrote. The seabed records something else: a very large number of small vessels carrying mixed cargoes along the coast, stopping at many ports and trading a little at each. Many of these boats were modest in size, able to carry a few hundred jars at most, and their crews probably owned a share of what they carried. This coastal traffic, dull enough to escape the attention of historians at the time, appears to have moved a far greater share of everyday goods than the famous fleets ever did.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The same evidence has been used to estimate how the scale of ancient trade changed over time. When the number of dated wrecks is plotted century by century, it rises steeply in the last centuries before the common era and falls sharply several hundred years later. Some economic historians have read this curve as a direct measure of commercial activity, a kind of trade figure written on the seabed. Others point out that it may partly reflect changes in packaging: once goods began to be shipped in wooden barrels rather than clay jars, sunken ships would have left far less to find, so that a fall in the number of known wrecks might mean a change in the way cargo was stored rather than a decline in the amount of it.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The greatest threat to this record is no longer the sea itself. Modern trawling drags heavy nets across the seabed and can flatten in a single pass a site that has lain undisturbed for two thousand years, while cheaper diving equipment has made the looting of shallow wrecks easier than ever. An international agreement adopted in 2001 obliges the countries that have signed it to protect underwater sites and discourages the commercial sale of their contents, but it has not been accepted everywhere, and enforcement far from shore remains difficult. Many archaeologists now argue that the most valuable thing to do with most wrecks is to record them thoroughly and then leave them where they lie.
paragraphs.label: G

texts.title: How the census learned to count

paragraphs.text: Governments have counted their people for as long as there have been governments, but for most of history they counted for narrow reasons and counted only the people who mattered for those reasons. Ancient states recorded men who could be taxed or called up to fight, and their records rarely listed women, children or the poor except as a total attached to the head of a household. Such counts were feared rather than welcomed, since being written down usually meant being made to pay, and families had every reason to hide their sons and understate their harvests. The results were therefore less a picture of the population than a picture of what the population was willing to reveal.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The modern census differs from these older counts in three respects: it aims to include everyone, it is repeated at regular intervals, and its results are published rather than kept for the private use of officials. These principles took hold gradually during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, when several European and American states began holding counts every ten years. Other countries followed much later, some of them only in the twentieth century. One of the earliest regular censuses was written into a national constitution, which required a count every decade so that seats in the national assembly could be shared out according to population. The count was therefore tied from the start to political representation rather than to taxation, and people had a reason to want to be included.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Counting everyone raised practical problems that no one had faced before. Enumerators, the officials who went from door to door, had to decide who belonged to a household, where travellers and sailors should be recorded, and how to count people who had no fixed home. Early instructions answered these questions differently from one country to another, and sometimes from one district to the next, so that figures from neighbouring areas could not be compared with any confidence. The solution that most countries eventually adopted was to count people wherever they spent a particular night, a rule which is simple to apply but which can inflate the population of a holiday town and reduce that of a city whose residents happen to be away.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The volume of paper was an even greater obstacle. As populations grew and the number of questions increased, clerks needed years to sort and total the returns by hand, and by the late nineteenth century one national census office calculated that it would barely finish tabulating one count before the next was due. The answer came from a machine that read holes punched in cards, each card standing for one person and each hole for one answer. Electrical contacts passed through the holes and advanced counters on a panel, and a count that would have taken most of a decade by hand was completed in a fraction of the time. The equipment developed for the census went on to become the foundation of office data processing for much of the following century.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: As the machinery improved, the questions multiplied. Censuses began to ask about occupation, birthplace, housing, language and, in some countries, ethnic origin. Each new question made the census more useful to planners, who needed to know where schools, hospitals and roads would be required, but it also made the exercise more contentious, because the categories offered on a form were never neutral. A question on language, for instance, might offer only the options that the state officially recognised, and people whose way of speaking fell outside them had either to choose a label that did not describe them or to leave the question blank. Other questions were added and then quietly withdrawn when it became clear that households understood them in too many different ways to produce figures that could be totalled.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: In recent decades the traditional census has come under pressure from two directions. Response rates have fallen in many countries, particularly in large cities, where people move frequently and are harder to find at home, and the cost of following up those who do not reply has risen sharply. In some large cities fewer than two thirds of households now return the form without a reminder. At the same time, governments already hold a great deal of information about residents in registers kept for tax, health care and education. A number of northern European countries have stopped sending out forms altogether and instead produce census results by linking these registers, a method that is far cheaper and can be repeated every year.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Not everyone is convinced that the old method should be abandoned. Registers record people as the administration sees them: someone who has left the country without telling anyone may remain on the books for years, while people who avoid officials may never appear at all. Critics also note that a register-based system depends on the public accepting that information supplied for one purpose may be combined and used for another. The census began as something to be feared and became, over two centuries, something most people accept as a public duty; whether that trust can be transferred to a system that never actually asks them anything remains an open question.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: In many countries that inherited their legal systems from England, serious criminal cases are still decided not by a judge but by twelve people chosen more or less at random from the public. The arrangement is centuries old, and it is regularly attacked as slow, expensive and unpredictable. Several countries that once relied on juries have abolished them or restricted them to a handful of cases, and in others the proportion of trials heard by a jury has been falling for decades. It is worth asking, then, whether the jury survives because it works or only because it is familiar. Its supporters, for their part, often defend it with sentiment rather than evidence, as if its age alone were a reason for keeping it.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The case against it usually begins with competence. Modern trials can involve weeks of technical evidence about finance, medicine or digital records, and it seems unreasonable to expect people with no training to follow all of it. The legal scholar Martin Hale, one of the jury’s sharper critics, argues that the problem is not intelligence but experience: a judge who has heard a hundred fraud cases knows which details matter, whereas a juror meeting the subject for the first time has to guess. He points out that in some long fraud trials the jury has been discharged after months because its members could no longer follow the case, forcing the whole process to begin again. Hale would keep juries for cases that turn on ordinary judgements of honesty and replace them with specialist panels wherever the evidence is highly technical.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: I think this argument is weaker than it looks. Studies in which mock juries are shown recordings of real trials have repeatedly found that their verdicts agree with the view of the presiding judge in most cases, around three quarters in the research I have seen. The finding is not new, and it has been repeated in countries with quite different legal traditions. Where the two disagree, it is usually because the jury was more reluctant to convict, not because it had misunderstood the evidence. Anna Kovacs, who has run several such studies, points out that jurors deliberate as a group, and that a group of twelve tends to correct the mistakes of any single member; a judge sitting alone has no such check.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: A more serious objection concerns what jurors bring into the room with them. Every juror has opinions formed long before the trial, and in an age when anyone can search for the name of a defendant on a phone, the rule that jurors must decide only on the evidence presented in court is hard to enforce. Some jurors, moreover, may not realise that looking up a defendant online is forbidden at all. Kovacs herself accepts that this is a genuine problem, though she notes that courts have responded with clearer instructions and, in some places, with criminal penalties for jurors who carry out their own research. Whether these measures work is difficult to know, since the discussions of a jury are secret and cannot be studied directly.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The case for the jury, in my view, rests less on accuracy than on legitimacy. A verdict reached by ordinary members of the public is harder to dismiss as the decision of a distant institution, and the knowledge that twelve strangers must be persuaded forces lawyers to explain the law in plain language. It also means that the law cannot easily drift too far from what ordinary people consider reasonable. The historian Daniel Osei has shown that juries have at times refused to convict people under laws they regarded as unjust, and that such refusals were sometimes followed by changes in the law itself. A judge, who is bound to apply the law as it is written, cannot perform this function, and nor, in fairness, should one.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: None of this means that the system cannot be improved. Jurors are still often expected to listen to days of evidence without taking notes or asking questions, a practice that makes little sense, and several courts that have allowed both have reported no loss of fairness as a result. The economist Priya Nair has estimated that a jury trial costs considerably more than a trial before a judge alone, mostly because it lasts longer; she suggests that much of the extra time is spent on procedure that exists to protect jurors from information rather than to help them understand it. Reducing that, she argues, would save more money than abolishing juries in a small number of complex cases.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: My own conclusion is that the jury’s critics are right about its costs and wrong about its value. We ask a great deal of ordinary people when we make them decide whether a fellow citizen has committed a crime, and they seem, on the whole, to carry out that duty conscientiously. They are not perfect, and no one seriously claims that they are. The strongest argument for keeping them is not that twelve people reach the right answer more often than one expert does, but that a society in which citizens take part in justice has a different relationship with its courts from one in which they merely watch.
paragraphs.label: G

groups.instruction: Text 1 has seven paragraphs, A–G. Choose the correct heading for paragraphs B–F from the list of headings below. Write the correct number, i–viii.

items.quote: a ship that sank in an afternoon is a single moment, sealed and left untouched, in which every object was in use on the same day
items.prompt: Everything recovered from a single wreck was in use at the same point in time.

explanation.en: “every object was in use on the same day” → TRUE: a wreck is one moment, unlike a city made of layered centuries.
explanation.kk: «every object was in use on the same day» → TRUE: кеме бір ғана сәтті сақтайды, ал қалада ғасырлар қабаттасып жатады.
explanation.ru: «every object was in use on the same day» → TRUE: корабль — один момент, в отличие от города, где слои веков лежат друг на друге.

items.quote: Metal corrodes into shapeless lumps, and glass slowly flakes away.
items.prompt: Glass is the material most likely to be found intact on an ancient wreck.

explanation.en: Glass “slowly flakes away”, while pottery is “almost indestructible”. The text names a different material, so the answer is FALSE, not NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Шыны «slowly flakes away», ал жойылмайтыны — керамика («Pottery, by contrast, is almost indestructible»). Мәтін басқа материалды нақты атайды, сондықтан NOT GIVEN емес, FALSE.
explanation.ru: Стекло «slowly flakes away», а почти неразрушима керамика («Pottery, by contrast, is almost indestructible»). Текст прямо называет другой материал — это FALSE, а не NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: the same timber lying on rock in shallow, warm water may disappear within a few decades, eaten by shipworm
items.prompt: Shipworm is present in all of the seas where ancient wrecks have been found.

explanation.en: The text only says shipworm eats timber in shallow, warm water. Whether it lives in every sea is never stated → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Жылы, таяз суда ағашты кеме құрты жейтіні ғана айтылған. Ол барлық теңізде бар ма, мәтінде жоқ → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Сказано только, что в тёплой мелкой воде древесину съедает корабельный червь. Во всех ли морях он есть, не сказано → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: divers working in short shifts at depths where the pressure limited them to minutes rather than hours
items.prompt: Twentieth-century excavators could spend only a limited time working on the seabed.

explanation.en: “the pressure limited them to minutes rather than hours” → TRUE: pressure kept shifts short.
explanation.kk: «the pressure limited them to minutes rather than hours» → TRUE: қысымға байланысты сүңгуірлер қысқа ауысыммен жұмыс істеген.
explanation.ru: «the pressure limited them to minutes rather than hours» → TRUE: из-за давления водолазы работали короткими сменами.

items.quote: Remotely operated vehicles can now work at depths that no diver could reach
items.prompt: Recording a wreck with underwater robots now costs less than excavating a site on land.

explanation.en: The vehicles reach great depths and allow precise measurement, but cost, and any comparison with land sites, is never mentioned → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Аппараттар сүңгуір жете алмайтын тереңдікте жұмыс істейді және орынды дәл өлшейді делінген. Бағасы мен құрлықтағы қазбамен салыстыру айтылмаған → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Об аппаратах сказано, что они работают на недоступной глубине и позволяют точно измерить место. О стоимости и сравнении с раскопками на суше — ни слова → NOT GIVEN.

explanation.ru: «An international agreement adopted in 2001» → 2001. «two thousand years» рядом — возраст памятника, а не дата соглашения.

explanation.kk: E абзацы: тіл туралы сұрақта тек ресми нұсқалар болса, кейбір адам өзіне сай емес белгіні таңдайды не сұрақты бос қалдырады → E. G абзацы да «көрінбейтін» адамдар туралы, бірақ ол тізілімдерге қатысты.
explanation.ru: Абзац E: если в вопросе о языке только официальные варианты, часть людей выбирает чужой ярлык или пропускает вопрос → E. В абзаце G тоже речь о тех, кого «не видно», но там про регистры, а не про варианты анкеты.

items.quote: someone who has left the country without telling anyone may remain on the books for years
items.prompt: a problem with records that are held by government departments

explanation.en: Paragraph G: registers keep people who have left and miss those who avoid officials → G. Paragraph F only presents registers as a cheaper method.
explanation.kk: G абзацы: тізілімде кетіп қалған адам жылдар бойы тұра береді, ал шенеуніктерден қашатындар мүлде жоқ → G. F абзацында тізілім тек арзан тәсіл ретінде сипатталады.
explanation.ru: Абзац G: в регистрах числится уехавший человек, а избегающих чиновников там нет совсем → G. В F регистры только описаны как дешёвый способ.

groups.instruction: Text 2 has seven paragraphs, A–G. Which paragraph contains the following information? Write the correct letter, A–G.

items.quote: its results are published rather than kept for the private use of officials
items.prompt: has its findings 19 ____

explanation.en: “its results are published rather than kept for the private use of officials” → published.
explanation.kk: «its results are published rather than kept for the private use of officials» → published.
explanation.ru: «its results are published rather than kept for the private use of officials» → published.

items.quote: The count was therefore tied from the start to political representation rather than to taxation
items.prompt: connected to political 20 ____

explanation.en: “tied from the start to political representation rather than to taxation” → representation. “taxation” is what it was not linked to.
explanation.kk: «tied from the start to political representation rather than to taxation» → representation. «taxation» — санақ дәл байланыспаған нәрсе.
explanation.ru: «tied from the start to political representation rather than to taxation» → representation. «taxation» — то, с чем перепись как раз НЕ была связана.

items.quote: produce census results by linking these registers
items.prompt: link existing 21 ____

explanation.en: “produce census results by linking these registers” → registers. The plural is needed: several registers are linked.
explanation.kk: «produce census results by linking these registers» → registers. Көпше түрі керек: бірнеше тізілім біріктіріледі.
explanation.ru: «produce census results by linking these registers» → registers. Нужна форма множественного числа: связывают несколько регистров.

items.quote: information supplied for one purpose may be combined and used for another
items.prompt: the one it was 22 ____ for

explanation.en: “information supplied for one purpose may be combined and used for another” → supplied.
explanation.kk: «information supplied for one purpose may be combined and used for another» → supplied.
explanation.ru: «information supplied for one purpose may be combined and used for another» → supplied.

groups.title: From counting to linking
groups.summary: Unlike earlier counts, the modern census tries to cover everyone, takes place at fixed intervals and has its findings 19 ____. In one early case the count was connected to political 20 ____ rather than to tax, so people had a motive to be counted. Today, lower response rates, especially in big cities, have made it more expensive to chase people who do not reply, and several countries now link existing 21 ____ instead of distributing forms. Critics worry that the public may not accept information being reused for a purpose other than the one it was 22 ____ for.
groups.instruction: Complete the summary below. Choose ONE WORD ONLY from Text 2 for each answer.

items.quote: The results were therefore less a picture of the population than a picture of what the population was willing to reveal.
items.prompt: What does the writer say about the results of ancient counts?

options.text: They were reliable for men but not for women.
They reflected what people were prepared to disclose.
They were shared with the households concerned.
They were repeated whenever taxes changed.

explanation.en: “less a picture of the population than a picture of what the population was willing to reveal” → B. A: reliability for men is not claimed; C and D are not mentioned.
explanation.kk: «less a picture of the population than a picture of what the population was willing to reveal» → B. A: ерлер туралы деректің сенімділігі айтылмаған; C мен D мәтінде жоқ.
explanation.ru: «less a picture of the population than a picture of what the population was willing to reveal» → B. A: о надёжности данных по мужчинам не сказано; C и D в тексте нет.

items.quote: so that figures from neighbouring areas could not be compared with any confidence
items.prompt: According to paragraph C, what was wrong with the first instructions given to enumerators?

options.text: They were too complicated for officials to follow.
They left travellers out of the count.
They differed so much that results could not be compared.
They were written only with large cities in mind.

explanation.en: Instructions varied between countries and districts, “so that figures from neighbouring areas could not be compared” → C. B is wrong: travellers were not left out; the issue was where to record them.
explanation.kk: Нұсқаулықтар әр елде, тіпті әр ауданда әртүрлі болған, «so that figures from neighbouring areas could not be compared» → C. B: саяхатшыларды шығармаған, оларды қай жерде жазу керек деген сұрақ болған.
explanation.ru: Инструкции отвечали на вопросы по-разному в разных странах и даже районах, «so that figures from neighbouring areas could not be compared» → C. B: путешественников не исключали — вопрос был, где их записать.

items.quote: a count that would have taken most of a decade by hand was completed in a fraction of the time
items.prompt: What was the main effect of the punched-card machine?

options.text: It made processing the returns far quicker.
It reduced the number of questions on the form.
It removed the need for door-to-door visits.
It prevented people from giving false answers.

explanation.en: “completed in a fraction of the time” → A. B is the opposite of what happened later; C and D are not mentioned.
explanation.kk: «completed in a fraction of the time» → A: санау әлдеқайда жылдам болды. B керісінше: кейін сұрақ көбейген; C мен D айтылмаған.
explanation.ru: «completed in a fraction of the time» → A: подсчёт стал во много раз быстрее. Об уменьшении вопросов (B) — наоборот, вопросов потом стало больше; C и D не упоминаются.

items.quote: a method that is far cheaper and can be repeated every year
items.prompt: Why have some northern European countries stopped sending out forms?

options.text: Residents refused to answer questions about language.
Registers were shown to be more accurate than forms.
The law no longer allowed personal questions.
Combining records already held costs much less.

explanation.en: The reason is cost and the chance to repeat it yearly → D. B is a trap: the text never says registers are more accurate, and critics in G point to their errors.
explanation.kk: Себеп — арзан және жыл сайын қайталауға болады → D. B — тұзақ: тізілімнің дәлдігі туралы айтылмаған, керісінше G абзацында сыншылар олардың қателігін көрсетеді.
explanation.ru: Причина — дешевле и можно повторять каждый год → D. B — ловушка: о большей точности регистров текст не говорит, а в G критики указывают как раз на их неточность.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

items.quote: Studies in which mock juries are shown recordings of real trials have repeatedly found
items.prompt: Research using recorded trials has been criticised because the cases were not live.

explanation.en: The writer reports studies using recordings of real trials and their findings, but says nothing about criticism of the method → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Автор нақты сот отырыстарының жазбасы бар зерттеулерді және олардың қорытындысын сипаттайды, бірақ бұл әдісті сынау туралы ештеңе айтпайды → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Автор описывает исследования с записями реальных процессов и их выводы, но о критике этого метода ничего не говорит → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: it is usually because the jury was more reluctant to convict, not because it had misunderstood the evidence
items.prompt: When a jury and a judge reach different conclusions, the jury has usually misread the evidence.

explanation.en: “usually because the jury was more reluctant to convict, not because it had misunderstood the evidence” → NO.
explanation.kk: «usually because the jury was more reluctant to convict, not because it had misunderstood the evidence» → NO: себеп — айыптауға асықпау, дәлелді түсінбеу емес.
explanation.ru: «usually because the jury was more reluctant to convict, not because it had misunderstood the evidence» → NO.

items.quote: in some places, with criminal penalties for jurors who carry out their own research
items.prompt: The punishments for jurors who investigate a case themselves are too severe.

explanation.en: The writer only notes that some places introduced such penalties; there is no view on their severity → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Кей жерлерде мұндай жаза енгізілгені ғана айтылған. Автор оның қатаңдығына баға бермейді → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Сказано лишь, что в некоторых местах такие наказания ввели. Оценки их строгости у автора нет → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: cannot perform this function, and nor, in fairness, should one
items.prompt: It is right that judges have no power to set aside a law they consider unfair.

explanation.en: “cannot perform this function, and nor, in fairness, should one” — the writer agrees a judge should not do this → YES.
explanation.kk: Судья «cannot perform this function, and nor, in fairness, should one» — автор судьяның заңды қолданбай қоя алмауын дұрыс деп санайды → YES.
explanation.ru: Судья «cannot perform this function, and nor, in fairness, should one» — автор считает правильным, что судья не может отказаться применять закон → YES.

items.quote: several courts that have allowed both have reported no loss of fairness as a result
items.prompt: Letting jurors take notes has made trials longer in the courts that permit it.

explanation.en: Courts reported no loss of fairness; nothing is said about trial length (Nair blames procedure, not note-taking) → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Соттар әділдік азаймағанын айтқан. Сот ұзақтығы туралы ештеңе жоқ; Nair бойынша сотты ұзартатын — жазба емес, рәсімдер → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Сказано, что суды не заметили потери справедливости. О длительности процессов ничего нет; удлиняют процесс, по Nair, процедуры, а не заметки → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: Several countries that once relied on juries have abolished them or restricted them to a handful of cases
items.prompt: Fewer countries use juries today than did so in the past.

explanation.en: “Several countries that once relied on juries have abolished them” → YES. No figures are given, but the decline itself is stated, so it is not NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: «Several countries that once relied on juries have abolished them» → YES. Нақты сан жоқ, бірақ азаю тікелей айтылған, сондықтан NOT GIVEN емес.
explanation.ru: «Several countries that once relied on juries have abolished them» → YES. Точных цифр нет, но само сокращение прямо названо — это не NOT GIVEN.

groups.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Text 3? Write YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer, NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer, NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this.

items.quote: a judge who has heard a hundred fraud cases knows which details matter
items.prompt: Familiarity with a type of case helps a professional see which facts are significant.

explanation.en: Hale: a judge who has heard a hundred fraud cases “knows which details matter” → A.
explanation.kk: Hale: жүз алаяқтық ісін қараған судья «knows which details matter» → A.
explanation.ru: Hale: судья, разобравший сотню дел о мошенничестве, «knows which details matter» → A.

items.quote: a group of twelve tends to correct the mistakes of any single member
items.prompt: Discussion within a group tends to cancel out the errors of individuals.

explanation.en: Kovacs: “a group of twelve tends to correct the mistakes of any single member” → B.
explanation.kk: Kovacs: «a group of twelve tends to correct the mistakes of any single member» → B.
explanation.ru: Kovacs: «a group of twelve tends to correct the mistakes of any single member» → B.

items.quote: such refusals were sometimes followed by changes in the law itself
items.prompt: Verdicts of not guilty have occasionally prompted the reform of laws.

explanation.en: Osei showed that juries’ refusals to convict were sometimes followed by changes in the law → C.
explanation.kk: Osei алқабилердің айыптаудан бас тартуы кейде заңның өзгеруіне әкелгенін көрсеткен → C.
explanation.ru: Osei показал, что отказы присяжных осуждать иногда вели к изменению закона → C.

items.quote: much of the extra time is spent on procedure that exists to protect jurors from information
items.prompt: Much of the extra expense comes from rules intended to keep information away from jurors.

explanation.en: Nair: the extra time goes on procedure that shields jurors from information → D. Kovacs discusses outside information too, but not cost.
explanation.kk: Nair: артық уақыт алқабилерді ақпараттан қорғайтын рәсімге кетеді → D. Kovacs та сырттағы ақпарат туралы айтады, бірақ шығын туралы емес.
explanation.ru: Nair: лишнее время уходит на процедуру, которая ограждает присяжных от информации → D. Kovacs тоже говорит о внешней информации, но о стоимости — нет.

options.text: Martin Hale
Anna Kovacs
Daniel Osei
Priya Nair

groups.instruction: Look at the following statements and the list of people below. Match each statement with the correct person, A–D.

items.quote: have abolished them or restricted them to a handful of cases
items.prompt: Some states where the jury was once the norm

explanation.en: “have abolished them or restricted them to a handful of cases” → A.
explanation.kk: «have abolished them or restricted them to a handful of cases» → A.
explanation.ru: «have abolished them or restricted them to a handful of cases» → A.

items.quote: replace them with specialist panels wherever the evidence is highly technical
items.prompt: According to Hale, panels of specialists

explanation.en: Hale would use specialist panels where evidence is highly technical → B. E is a trap: acquittals in fraud cases are never mentioned.
explanation.kk: Hale дәлелдер тым техникалық болғанда арнайы алқа құруды ұсынады → B. E — тұзақ: алаяқтық істері бойынша ақтау туралы айтылмаған.
explanation.ru: Hale предлагает специальные коллегии там, где доказательства сугубо технические → B. E — ловушка: об оправданиях по делам о мошенничестве не сказано.

items.quote: Whether these measures work is difficult to know, since the discussions of a jury are secret
items.prompt: The fact that jury discussions are kept confidential

explanation.en: “Whether these measures work is difficult to know, since the discussions of a jury are secret” → C.
explanation.kk: «Whether these measures work is difficult to know, since the discussions of a jury are secret» → C.
explanation.ru: «Whether these measures work is difficult to know, since the discussions of a jury are secret» → C.

items.quote: the knowledge that twelve strangers must be persuaded forces lawyers to explain the law in plain language
items.prompt: Having to win over members of the public

explanation.en: “twelve strangers must be persuaded forces lawyers to explain the law in plain language” → D.
explanation.kk: «twelve strangers must be persuaded forces lawyers to explain the law in plain language» → D.
explanation.ru: «twelve strangers must be persuaded forces lawyers to explain the law in plain language» → D.

would suit trials that depend on highly technical evidence.
makes it hard to judge whether rules against outside research are effective.

are more likely to acquit than to convict in fraud cases.
